voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: To us Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true. The Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

glosses.plain_meaning: The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. It is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ.
glosses.quick_meaning: The Single One: our word for the vowed celibate - and, at the same time, our title for Christ the Only-Begotten.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Solitary' misleads: the ihidaye lived among the congregation, not in isolation; the singleness is of heart and allegiance, not of address.
false_friend: monk (the later, drifted sense of the word)

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: He healed the sick and taught in parables. He gathered disciples and sent them out. He broke bread with his own and gave them the cup. The harmony we read in worship - the one continuous Gospel story - carried all of this. What we preached above all was the rescue: he went into death's country, broke its rule, and came out. Our hymns show Death himself trembling that his house has been plundered. He took sin and nailed it to his cross. By rising he became the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead. We sang of him as the Physician whose coming was medicine for a wounded people. The harmony itself no longer survives whole - only in fragments and later translations. What we can tell you is what we preached from it, not a verse-by-verse account of everything the text said he did.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
Ihidaya - the Single One. One word does two things at once among us. It names the vowed celibate, the man or woman who lives single-minded and undivided for God. And it is also our Syriac title for Christ himself, as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, yhd, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ. Ephrem wrote: “The Only-Begotten left his place with God. He made his home in the Virgin, so that, by a common manner of birth, though only-begotten, he might become the brother of many.”

The word carries both at once. When we sang of the Ihidaya dwelling in the Virgin, we meant the Only-Begotten Son. When we spoke of an ihidaya keeping the fast, we meant a covenant member bound to celibacy for life. It is not that the word drifted from one meaning to another. Both senses belonged to it from the beginning, held together in one term.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
We believed it because we received it as preaching, and because we staked our lives on it. A century and more stood between us and the events themselves. We claimed no living eyewitnesses. What we had was the Gospel woven into one continuous story, the harmony we read in worship. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. We held that every old word the prophets, kings, and priests had carried came true the day he was born. Ephrem sang: "This is the day that gladdened the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests, for in it were fulfilled all the things they had spoken: “This is the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad. On this day their words came true - all of them. For on this day the Virgin gave birth to Immanuel in Bethlehem.”

And the whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead. Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died. We also believed it by answering those who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus. Against Bardaisan and Mani we argued in the same streets, often in the same verse forms. Knowing what we believed meant knowing what we refused.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: The one we can give you most fully is Ephrem himself, our poet and deacon. He taught at Nisibis while it still belonged to Rome, then walked to Edessa when the city was ceded to Persia in 363. He never left again. He spent his last years writing madrashe - teaching hymns - that the daughters of the covenant sang in the churches. Every doctrine we held, he taught by singing it: the Only-Begotten dwelling in the Virgin, the font as a womb, Eden and the cross read as type answering type. The early tradition tells that in the famine of his last year he nursed the starving in Edessa's public porches, and died soon after the famine ended. What we know for certain is his diaconate and the fact that the choirs sang his hymns. Later people said he founded and led the women's choirs himself, but that tradition appears only around 500 - generations after he died. He lived what he sang: the Single One, single-minded for God.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: That our teaching was meant to be sung, not merely read. Doctrine among us was carried in the madrasha - the teaching hymn with its stanzas and refrain. The melody and the words together carried the argument into the body, so people learned what we believed by keeping the tune. Ephrem wrote hymn after hymn this way, and the daughters of the covenant sang them in every congregation. When we taught that Jesus is the Only-Begotten who dwelt in the Virgin, or that the font is a womb for the second birth, we sang it first. The singing was not decoration beside the real teaching. It was the teaching itself. And I would want you to know that we held truth and symbol as one bound pair: raza and shrara, the symbol and the truth it carries. Eden pointed to the cross, the Jordan to the font, Adam to Christ. A raza was not a stand-in chosen at will. It was bound to the truth it showed. We read Scripture and the world this way, through signs that carried hidden depths.
